readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module tours the AWS database portfolio, starting with how the shared responsibility model splits database work into fully managed, managed and unmanaged. It covers relational options (Amazon RDS, Amazon Aurora and AWS DMS for migrations), the NoSQL service Amazon DynamoDB and a console demo of both RDS and DynamoDB. It then adds in-memory caching with Amazon ElastiCache and purpose-built databases (Amazon DocumentDB, Amazon Neptune, Amazon Managed Blockchain and DynamoDB Accelerator). It ends with AWS Backup, a backup service that protects databases and storage alike.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 7 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Databases: who handles which database tasks under fully managed, managed and unmanaged services, and when self-hosting on EC2 makes sense.

AWS Database Services

  1. Relational Database Services: relational databases and SQL, lift-and-shift with AWS DMS, Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora.
  2. NoSQL Database Services: flexible-schema key-value databases and Amazon DynamoDB with its global tables and auto scaling.
  3. AWS Databases Demonstration: building an RDS for MySQL database and a DynamoDB table in the console, and how the two differ.
  4. In-Memory Caching Services: why caches relieve database bottlenecks and how Amazon ElastiCache works alongside a database.
  5. Additional Database Services: purpose-built databases (DocumentDB, Neptune, Managed Blockchain, DAX) and AWS Backup for central backups.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Fully managed databases leave you only data structure design and access control, while self-managing on Amazon EC2 pays off only when you need OS-level control.
  • Relational databases use a rigid schema of related tables and SQL, and NoSQL databases differ mainly by using flexible schemas.
  • Amazon RDS automates patching, backups and failover for operational workloads, and Multi-AZ deployments keep it available.
  • Amazon Aurora delivers commercial-grade performance at about one-tenth the cost, with up to 5x MySQL throughput and six copies across three AZs.
  • AWS DMS minimizes application downtime because the source database stays live during migration.
  • Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond latency and auto scaling that follows real traffic.
  • Amazon ElastiCache complements a database with in-memory caching, offloading reads and allowing smaller instances.
  • Amazon DocumentDB serves semistructured JSON documents with MongoDB compatibility, and Amazon Neptune serves highly connected graph data.
  • AWS Backup centralizes backup policies across AWS services, accounts, Regions and on-premises resources.
  • AWS recommends a purpose-built database for each workload rather than one database for everything.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

  • The thread running through the module is matching each workload to the right database, with AWS taking on more of the operations the more managed the service is.
  • For structured, transactional data, Amazon RDS is the starting point, Aurora steps in when you want commercial-grade speed and availability for less, and AWS DMS gets existing databases there without a long outage.
  • When schemas need to flex or traffic is huge, DynamoDB is the NoSQL choice, while DocumentDB fits JSON documents and Neptune fits relationship-heavy graphs.
  • When reads swamp a database, ElastiCache adds a memory layer next to it, and AWS Backup ties the protection of all these data stores together in one place.

relational-database-services.html:
Relational Database Services

Objectives

  • Explain what a is.
  • Describe and , their benefits and their use cases.

Notes

Relational databases

  • Transactional data, like the coffee shop's orders and loyalty records, usually sits in a relational database management system.
    • Spotting repeat drink orders lets the shop send a discount.
  • Tables of rows and columns follow a rigid schema and share attributes, so one query spans customers and orders.
  • is the usual interface, on engines like MySQL, PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server, and the model keeps structured data consistent and scalable.
  • AWS's fully managed relational options remove admin work but keep availability and security, and familiar engines (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle) ease migration.

Moving an existing database

  • puts an on-premises database as is on , keeping control of OS, memory, CPU and storage.
  • eases the move and minimizes app downtime, since the source stays live throughout.

Amazon RDS

  • A relational service for operational workloads, not data warehousing, that automates patching, backups, provisioning, failover and disaster recovery.
  • The course labels RDS and Aurora both managed and fully managed.
  • AWS runs infrastructure, OS, patching and backups, while you own security measures and and in transit.
  • Instance classes favor memory, performance or I/O, scaling is vertical or horizontal, and storage is not fixed.
  • Engines: Aurora, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server and Oracle Database.
  • Resilience: Multi-AZ, automated backups on your schedule, and manual DB snapshots (full copies for or archives).
  • Use cases: web apps, enterprise workloads, e-commerce inventories.
Benefit How
Cost No hardware, pay-as-you-go, less admin
Multi-AZ A standby in another AZ takes over automatically
Performance Read replicas offload reads, shows live load
Security VPC isolation, encryption, backups, Multi-AZ

Amazon Aurora

  • MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible, built to cut needless I/O (the video also lists distributed SQL, DSQL).
  • About one-tenth the cost of high-end commercial databases at similar performance, so it suits replacing pricey commercial engines.
  • Up to 5x MySQL and 3x PostgreSQL throughput comes from distributed storage, not automatic CPU scaling.
  • Storage grows on its own from 10 GB to 128 TB, backed up continuously to , encrypted at rest and continuously monitored.
  • Six copies over three AZs, 99.99% availability, failover to healthy replicas without data loss, and up to 15 Aurora Replicas.
  • Through , point-in-time restore reaches back up to 35 days.
  • Use cases: games, media and content management, real-time analytics.
  • Overkill for temporary dev or rarely read data, and not for unstructured streams.

Visuals

  • Inventory table: one coffee product per row with ID, name, size and price.
  • Benefit accordions: four RDS and three Aurora panels, summarized above.

Key takeaways

  • Relational databases pair a rigid schema with SQL and suit transactional data.
  • AWS DMS minimizes downtime by keeping the source live.
  • RDS automates upkeep for operational workloads, while you own security and encryption.
  • Multi-AZ fails RDS over to a standby automatically.
  • Aurora matches commercial databases at about a tenth of the cost.

Scenarios

  • Rewarding repeat orders: relate customer and order tables.
  • Keeping a familiar setup in the cloud: lift-and-shift to EC2, with AWS DMS.
  • Knowledge checks practise RDS Multi-AZ for always-on data and Aurora's storage design for peak MySQL load.

Terms

  • Relational database: related tables under a fixed schema.
  • SQL: the language for querying relational data.
  • Lift-and-shift: moving a database unchanged onto EC2.
  • AWS DMS: a migration service that keeps the source running.
  • Amazon RDS: AWS's relational database service with automated upkeep.
  • Multi-AZ deployment: a standby in another AZ that takes over on failure.
  • DB snapshot: a manual full backup of an RDS instance.
  • Read replica: a copy that takes read traffic off the primary.
  • Performance Insights: real-time RDS load analysis.
  • Amazon Aurora: a high-throughput MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible database.
  • Aurora Replica: one of up to 15 cluster copies that traffic can fail over to.

nosql-database-services.html:
NoSQL Database Services

Objectives

  • Explain NoSQL databases.
  • Describe , its benefits and use cases.

Notes

Relational versus NoSQL

  • Relational databases (MySQL, say), long the default, need a set schema and .
  • In certain cases they struggle to perform or scale, and fixed schemas suit changing attributes poorly.
  • NoSQL (nonrelational) databases hold key-value pairs: a unique key names an item and attributes carry its values, like a dictionary headword and definition.
  • Items can differ in attributes, which come and go freely (one customer has a favorite drink, another a birthday).
  • The core difference is flexible versus rigid schema, not speed or scaling, and NoSQL still indexes the primary key by default.

Amazon DynamoDB

  • Fully managed, serverless NoSQL for key-value and document data.
  • Single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, with no patching, upgrades, maintenance windows, downtime or cold starts.
  • Data spreads over many servers and SSDs with no practical size cap, you pay per use, and security is built in.
  • Use cases: gaming, finance and global mobile apps, served worldwide by global tables.
  • Auto scaling with provisioned capacity: throughput automatically follows real use toward your target utilization, steady at peaks, cheaper when quiet.
  • Availability: 99.999%, copies in three facilities per Region and in other Regions.
  • Encryption: automatic at rest and in transit, with a choice of keys.
  • Pick it for speed, changeable schemas and offloaded management.

Visuals

  • Key-value table: two items with different attributes.
  • Accordion: four benefit panels.

Key takeaways

  • NoSQL differs from relational mainly by flexible schemas.
  • DynamoDB is serverless, single-digit millisecond fast and maintenance-free.
  • Auto scaling avoids the waste or slow peaks of hand-set read/write capacity.

Scenarios

  • Prime Day 2024 on global tables: tens of trillions of calls in 48 hours, peaking at 146 million requests per second.
  • A knowledge check matches unpredictable traffic to auto scaling.

Terms

  • NoSQL database: a nonrelational, flexible-schema database.
  • Key-value pair: a unique key plus an item's attributes.
  • Item and attribute: a DynamoDB record and its name-value pairs, with values such as numbers, sets or documents.
  • Amazon DynamoDB: AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database.
  • DynamoDB global tables: the feature for worldwide DynamoDB apps, as on Prime Day.

aws-databases-demonstration.html:
AWS Databases Demonstration

Objectives

  • Launch an instance in the and use to build and fill tables.
  • Create a DynamoDB table in the console, add items, then it.

Notes

Amazon RDS in the console

  • Setup is a handful of choices: the MySQL engine, the for trials, an identifier (database-1), admin credentials and the default VPC.
  • Public access was turned on only so a SQL client could reach it, and real systems allow just authorized apps.
  • Once the status reads available, a client connects with the from the connectivity and security tab plus the credentials.
  • SQL then created users, products and orders tables tied by foreign keys, inserted rows, and joined them to list one user's orders.
  • Every row had to fill the same columns, showing the rigid schema.

Amazon DynamoDB in the console

  • A table needs only a name (orders) and a (order number, type Number), and is usable once active.
  • Each item must carry a partition key value, while its other attributes can vary.
  • Apps reach DynamoDB by calling its APIs through the , as a Python script did to load 10 items.
  • A scan (Explore table items, then Run) read back everything, and a notes attribute appeared on only some items.
  • A for order number 5 returned that single item, the better tool as tables grow.

RDS versus DynamoDB

Amazon RDS
You work with An instance holding related tables Stand-alone tables, no instances
Schema Rigid, same columns per row Flexible, only the partition key required
Linking data Foreign keys and joins No foreign keys
Querying SQL Its own query language
App access Client via endpoint, port, credentials AWS SDK calls to DynamoDB APIs

Key takeaways

  • An RDS database takes a few console choices, and clients connect via endpoint, port and credentials.
  • RDS links rigid tables with foreign keys, and DynamoDB tables stand alone with flexible schemas.
  • A DynamoDB table needs just a name and a partition key.
  • A scan returns the whole table, while a query fetches items by partition key.

Scenarios

  • Just trying RDS out: use the free tier template.
  • Letting a demo SQL client connect: enable public access, then lock it down in production.
  • Finding one order in a growing table: query the partition key instead of scanning.

Terms

  • Free tier template: an RDS setup preset for trying the service.
  • DB instance identifier: an RDS instance's name, such as database-1.
  • Endpoint and port: the address clients use to reach an RDS instance.
  • Foreign key: the link relating one RDS table to another, absent in DynamoDB.
  • Partition key: the required attribute that identifies DynamoDB items and that a query looks up.
  • Scan: a DynamoDB read of every item in a table.
  • Query: a DynamoDB read of the items matching a partition key value.
  • AWS SDK: what application code uses to invoke DynamoDB's APIs.

in-memory-caching-services.html:
In-Memory Caching Services

Objectives

  • Explain in-memory caching and how it helps databases.
  • Describe , its benefits and use cases.

Notes

Why databases slow down

  • Growth brings read floods and heavy queries on big datasets, bottlenecking relational back ends like .
  • Read-heavy traffic for data that rarely changes is common, and a is one of the best remedies.

In-memory caches

  • A cache keeps hot data in RAM, which reads hundreds to thousands of times faster than disk.
  • Typical contents: sessions, responses, query results, anything requested repeatedly.
  • Lacking a database's lasting storage and rich queries, a cache complements the database, never replaces it.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, What is Amazon ElastiCache? The exam guide calls in-memory data stores memory-based databases, and its example is Amazon ElastiCache, a managed in-memory data store and cache.

Amazon ElastiCache

  • Fully managed caching compatible with , so existing tools keep working.
  • Sub-millisecond reads and writes (the video says microsecond reads).
  • You resize the cache with demand, or let the serverless option scale itself, while AWS runs the infrastructure.
  • It scales the cache only, not the database's storage.
  • Reading from the cache can let you run smaller, cheaper database instances.
  • Meant for frequently read data, not cheap storage of cold data, network links or secrets.
  • Use cases: session data, faster queries, game leaderboards.
Benefit How
Performance AWS provisions, patches, monitors; you add or remove nodes
Failed nodes replaced, a replica promoted, usually in minutes
Multi-AZ replication Primary and replicas in separate AZs survive a zone outage
Encryption At rest on disks and backups, in transit via

Where ElastiCache sits

  • EC2 runs the app, RDS is the database, and ElastiCache sits alongside both.
  • The app tries the cache first and returns any hit at once.
  • On a miss, it reads RDS, caches the result and replies, so the next request hits.

Visuals

  • Caching architecture (video): a request trying ElastiCache before RDS.
  • Benefits accordion: the four panels in the table above.

Key takeaways

  • Caching keeps hot data in RAM, checked before the database, for very low latency and less load.
  • ElastiCache complements, never replaces, the database.
  • A cache can allow smaller database instances.

Scenarios

  • Shoppers flooding one product page: cache it so RDS stops repeating a query.
  • A gaming platform: fast leaderboards and real-time analytics.
  • A content delivery system: popular data served quickly.
  • A knowledge check practises the latency and throughput bottlenecks ElastiCache solves.

Terms

  • In-memory cache: a RAM layer holding hot data temporarily.
  • Caching layer: a cache alongside a database that answers repeat reads.
  • Amazon ElastiCache: AWS's fully managed in-memory cache.
  • Redis OSS, Valkey and Memcached: caching tools ElastiCache supports.
  • ElastiCache serverless: an option that scales with demand by itself.
  • Replica node: a copy promoted if the primary fails.
  • TLS: transport layer security for client-to-cache traffic.

additional-database-services.html:
Additional Database Services

Objectives

  • Describe , and , with benefits and use cases.

Notes

Purpose-built databases

  • Fit the database to the business need, not the data to the database, as none suits every job.
  • AWS steers each workload to its best-fit purpose-built tool, and offers more than the course covers.

Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)

  • Where DynamoDB handles key-value data, DocumentDB takes too complex for rows and columns.
  • Fully managed, it stores, queries and indexes JSON-like documents with dynamic schemas, ideal when schemas change often.
  • Continuous backup and enterprise-grade security come built in.
  • Use cases: content management, catalogs and inventory, user profiles and personalization.
  • Not ideal for strict-compliance banking (relational fits better), archives or in-memory caching.
  • MongoDB compatibility: MongoDB APIs, drivers, tools, code and skills carry over with few changes.
  • Scaling: storage grows on its own in 10 GB steps to 64 TB, compute scales either way, and it serves millions of requests per second.
  • Read throughput: up to 15 replicas share storage.

Amazon Neptune

  • A fully managed for highly connected data, like social webs that are clumsy in relational tables.
  • Low-latency queries and high-throughput reads and writes suit real-time apps, with automatic failover and backups.
  • Use cases: social network mapping, fraud detection, search and recommendations.
  • Not for general streaming analytics, replacing all databases, or document text search.
  • Relationships: property graph and RDF (Resource Description Framework) models for mapping relationships and matching patterns.
  • Scale: billions of relationships in milliseconds as complexity grows, storage up to 64 TB, and a traversal-tuned engine.

Other specialized options

  • runs blockchain networks, such as a grocer's food-safety shipment tracking.
  • is a built-in cache that sharply cuts DynamoDB read times.

AWS Backup

  • A backup service for databases and storage alike, not a database.
  • Separate disk and database backup plans overlap and confuse, so it unifies them in one dashboard.
  • It covers EBS, , RDS, DynamoDB and more, even on-premises data.
  • Use cases: central disaster recovery, consistent compliance policies, one backup interface.
  • Central management: one view of jobs, restore points and compliance across services and accounts, with schedules, encryption and auto-protection of new resources.
  • Cross-Region redundancy: copies in other Regions allow restores during a Regional outage.
  • Compliance: audit logs, reports, organization-wide policies and activity tracking.

Visuals

  • Benefit accordions: eight panels across the three services.

Key takeaways

  • Use purpose-built databases, since none fits every workload.
  • DocumentDB stores semistructured JSON with MongoDB compatibility.
  • Neptune answers fast when data is a dense web of relationships.
  • AWS Backup centralizes backups across services, accounts, Regions and on premises.

Scenarios

  • Mapping a social network: Neptune.
  • A grocer tracing shipments: Managed Blockchain.
  • Backups scattered over EBS, EFS, RDS and DynamoDB: AWS Backup.

Terms

  • Purpose-built database: one designed for a specific workload.
  • Semistructured data: varied, complex data that defies rigid schemas.
  • Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility): a fully managed MongoDB-compatible document database.
  • Amazon Neptune: a fully managed graph database.
  • Graph database: one built around connections.
  • Amazon Managed Blockchain: a service for building and running blockchain networks.
  • DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX): a built-in DynamoDB cache.
  • AWS Backup: central, automated backup for AWS and on-premises data.

labs.title: Cache the menu
labs.brief: At lunch the cafe's app reads the same menu 900 times a second and writes 50 orders a second to one small Amazon RDS database. Choose the database size and the cache so menu reads average at most 10 ms, the database keeps spare capacity and the month costs at most 200 lab credits. Every figure in this lab is a lab value: a read takes 0.5 ms from the cache and 20 ms from the database, writes always reach the database, and a database slows sharply once its load passes its capacity.

goals.label: Menu reads average 10 ms or less
goals.hint: A bigger database still fetches every read from disk itself; only reads answered from memory before the database is asked come back much faster.

goals.label: The database keeps spare capacity at lunch
goals.hint: Database load is every read that reaches it plus every write, and a flood of repeated reads for the same menu need not reach the database at all.

goals.label: The month costs at most 200 lab credits
goals.hint: Every database and cache is billed each month, and once repeated reads are answered before the database, it no longer has to be sized for the whole lunch flood.

lines: With the cache answering most menu reads, only the misses and the writes reached the small database, so it stopped bottlenecking under the lunch flood.
A read from the in-memory cache returns far faster than one from the database's disk, so latency fell, while a bigger database alone still served every read from disk.
Because the cache took the repeated reads, the small database was enough, and the small database with the cache cost less than the large database by itself.
The cache complements the database rather than replacing it, since a miss is read from the database and cached for the next request, and the database keeps the lasting data.

goals.hint: Ask which upkeep AWS has taken off the cafe's hands, and which setup and tuning work the cafe still does itself.

goals.label: The serverless services and the cafe's small share sit under Fully managed
goals.hint: Ask whether any server is left for the cafe to see at all, or only its own data design, access and code.

lines: On Amazon EC2, AWS runs only the physical layer, so installing, patching, backing up and scaling the database are the cafe's jobs.
Amazon RDS hands patching and backups to AWS, but the cafe still configures the database and tunes its queries.
Amazon DynamoDB and AWS Lambda hide every server, leaving the cafe its data design, access and code.
The more the cafe hands to AWS, the less it can tweak and the less it has to look after, so each workload gets the model that fits it.

questions.takeaway: A database you install on EC2 leaves patching of both the database and its OS with you, unlike a managed service such as RDS.

read.text: With EC2 hosted databases you still install, patch, back up and scale the database and its operating system yourself, while AWS managed databases such as Amazon RDS hand those tasks to AWS.

questions.stem: The cafe's loyalty records live in a MySQL database installed on an Amazon EC2 instance. Who applies the security patches to that database and to the server's operating system?

options.text: AWS for both
options.why: AWS patches only what it manages, and a database installed on an EC2 instance is not managed by AWS.

options.text: The cafe for both
options.why: On a self-hosted EC2 database the cafe installs, patches, backs up and scales both the database and its OS.

options.text: AWS for the OS, the cafe for MySQL
options.why: With the database hosted on EC2, the operating system is also the cafe's job, not something AWS patches.

options.text: The cafe for the OS, AWS for MySQL
options.why: AWS does not patch database software the cafe installed itself on an EC2 instance.

questions.takeaway: A managed service removes daily operations, but some provisioning, like choosing server size, can still fall to the customer.

read.text: Managed: AWS absorbs much of the operational overhead, though some provisioning or configuration may remain yours depending on the service.

questions.stem: The cafe sets up a database service on AWS, and its team must choose the server size and storage up front. After that, AWS patches and operates the service day to day. Which service model does this describe?

options.text: An unmanaged service
options.why: An unmanaged service would leave patching and daily operation with the cafe, but AWS does that work here.

options.text: A managed service
options.why: A managed service takes over the daily operation while leaving some provisioning, such as server size, with the customer.

options.text: A fully managed service
options.why: A fully managed service leaves no servers to provision, yet here the cafe has to pick the server size itself.

options.text: An on-premises service
options.why: An on-premises service runs on the cafe's own hardware, so AWS would not be patching or operating it.

questions.takeaway: With a fully managed service like Lambda, AWS handles scaling for demand spikes, so the customer provisions no capacity.

read.text: Fully managed, like serverless Lambda: there are no servers for you to provision or manage, and AWS also covers scaling and availability.

questions.stem: The cafe runs its order-confirmation logic on AWS Lambda, a fully managed service. A weekend promotion is expected to bring a large rush of orders. Who makes sure the logic has enough capacity for the rush?

options.text: The cafe's developers
options.why: The developers own the function code, but capacity under a fully managed service is not part of their share.

options.text: The cafe's ops staff
options.why: With a fully managed service there are no servers for the cafe to provision, so its ops staff have nothing to add.

options.text: AWS on its own
options.why: Under a fully managed service like Lambda, AWS alone covers scaling, so the extra orders get capacity without the cafe acting.

options.text: The cafe and AWS jointly
options.why: Scaling is not shared here, since a fully managed service puts it wholly with AWS.

incidents.title: The promotion that slowed the order lookup
incidents.brief: The cafe's ordering app keeps every order in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and a weekend promotion launches on Friday. The team has a short list: record promo details, fix a save that keeps failing and speed up the staff screen that finds one order.

steps.takeaway: A flexible schema lets new items add attributes that older items lack, with no table-wide change made first.

read.text: Items can differ in attributes, which come and go freely (one customer has a favorite drink, another a birthday).

steps.stem: Starting Friday, promo orders will also record the promo code used, which ordinary orders never had. Why can the app save its first promo order without any change to the table beforehand?

options.text: Items in one table can hold different attributes
options.why: Each DynamoDB item carries its own set of attributes, so promo orders simply include the code and older orders stay as they are.

options.text: No servers need patching, since DynamoDB is serverless
options.why: Being serverless removes patching and maintenance, but it says nothing about items gaining a field that older items lack.

options.text: Data is encrypted at rest and in transit automatically
options.why: Automatic encryption protects the stored orders, but it does not explain how a new field can appear on some items only.

options.text: Throughput follows real traffic through auto scaling
options.why: Auto scaling helps with the promotion's extra traffic, but it does not let items hold a field the others lack.

steps.takeaway: Every DynamoDB item must include the partition key value, while all of its other attributes are optional.

read.text: Each item must carry a partition key value, while its other attributes can vary.

steps.stem: The orders table identifies each order by its order number. A test promo order keeps failing to save: the item holds a drink name, a price and a promo code, but no order number. Why is the item rejected?

options.text: Every item must hold a value for the partition key
options.why: Each DynamoDB item must carry a value for the partition key, here the order number, so an item without one is refused.

options.text: Tables stand alone, with no foreign keys to others
options.why: It is true that DynamoDB tables have no foreign keys, but nothing here tries to link the item to another table.

options.text: Apps call the DynamoDB APIs through the AWS SDK
options.why: The SDK is how the app sends the item, but the way it is sent does not decide whether the item is accepted.

options.text: A new table is usable once its status is active
options.why: The orders table is already in use for ordinary orders, so its status is not what blocks this one item.

steps.takeaway: A query fetches items by their partition key value, so finding one order in a growing table means querying that key, not scanning.

read.text: A query for order number 5 returned that single item, the better tool as tables grow.

steps.stem: Each order item holds its order number, which is the table's partition key, and a receipt number printed on the customer's slip. The staff screen finds one order by reading every item in the table and picking out the match, and now that the table has grown it is slow. Which read should the screen use instead?

options.text: A scan for the receipt number
options.why: A scan reads every item in the table whatever value it looks for, which is the slow behavior the screen already has.

options.text: A query for the order number
options.why: A query fetches only the items matching a partition key value, and the order number is that key, so the lookup stays quick.

options.text: A query for the receipt number
options.why: A query looks items up by the partition key value, and the receipt number is an ordinary attribute rather than that key.

options.text: A scan for the order number
options.why: Even with the right value to match, a scan still reads every item before picking one out, so the screen stays slow.
